c.tagline: Faded grandeur, classic cars, and salsa on every corner.

taxi.color: yellow (state Cubataxi) or classic American cars
taxi.fareNote: Most tourist taxis negotiate a fixed fare upfront in USD/CUP cash before departure; official yellow Cubataxi cabs sometimes use meters but fixed pricing is far more common.

emergency.note: Tourist-specific assistance also available via Asistur at +53 7 866-4499; response times and resources are limited compared to North America/Europe.

avoid.reason: Low violent crime; petty theft/scams in Habana Vieja and Centro Habana — mind bags and touts (jineteros)

hood_desc: The historic UNESCO-listed core with cobblestone plazas, colonial architecture, and the highest concentration of restored hotels, restaurants, and museums; best for first-time visitors who want to walk everywhere.

A leafy, seafront district of 1950s mansions, university buildings, and the iconic Malecón and Hotel Nacional; suits travelers wanting a residential feel with easy access to nightlife and casas particulares.
A grittier, densely populated area right by Old Havana with cheap paladares and local life on display; good for budget travelers who don't mind a rougher edge and lots of street noise.

An upscale, leafy diplomatic and business district west of the Almendares River with modern hotels, embassies, and better infrastructure; suits business travelers and those wanting quiet and reliability.

A working port town across Havana Bay reached by ferry, home to Che Guevara's mausoleum-adjacent sites and a laid-back, less touristy vibe; suits day-trippers or those seeking a quieter, cheaper base.
lodging: Gran Hotel Manzana Kempinski La Habana

water.note: Avoid tap water; drink only bottled or boiled water.

transit.pay: Fares on regular city buses are paid in cash CUP directly to the driver or a conductor (very low fixed fare); the harbor ferry to Regla/Casablanca is also a small cash CUP fare paid at the dock. Tourist hop-on-hop-off buses (Habana Bus Tour) are paid in USD/CUP cash or card at kiosks.
transit.hours: City buses run roughly 5:00-24:00 with reduced frequency at night; the ferry operates until around 22:00-23:00; taxis and classic-car cabs are the main night option.
transit.note: Public buses are often extremely crowded and unpredictable due to fuel shortages; most visitors rely on taxis, pre-arranged transfers, or walking within neighborhoods rather than city buses.

train: Ferrocarriles de Cuba national rail from Havana Central Station (limited, slow service to other provinces)
ferry: Havana Bay ferry to Regla and Casablanca

tip.r: Service staff earn very low state wages in CUP, so tips (ideally in cash USD or EUR) are a major part of income; 10% is typical at restaurants, and small tips for musicians, guides, and casa particular hosts are strongly expected.

landmarks: El Capitolio
This grand neoclassical dome, once the seat of Cuba's government, dominates Havana's skyline and is famous for closely resembling the U.S. Capitol building.
Malecón
This five-mile seaside esplanade and seawall is Havana's beloved gathering spot, where locals and tourists watch waves crash at sunset against a backdrop of faded pastel buildings.
Havana Cathedral
Set in a baroque plaza in Old Havana, this 18th-century cathedral with its asymmetrical twin bell towers is considered one of the finest examples of Cuban baroque architecture.
Morro Castle (Castillo del Morro)
Guarding Havana's harbor entrance since 1589, this fortress with its iconic lighthouse offers sweeping views and is a must-photograph symbol of the city's colonial defenses.
Gran Teatro de La Habana
This ornate Belle Époque theater, home to the Cuban National Ballet, dazzles visitors with elaborate sculptural facades and marks the heart of Havana's cultural life.
Hotel Nacional de Cuba
This legendary 1930s hotel perched above the Malecón has hosted mobsters, movie stars, and world leaders, making its gardens and Art Deco lobby essential Havana stops.
Plaza Vieja
One of Havana's four original colonial squares, this lively plaza charms visitors with restored 17th-century mansions, a colorful fountain, and open-air cafes.
Plaza de la Revolución
This vast public square is instantly recognizable for the giant steel Che Guevara mural on the Ministry of the Interior, a global icon of revolutionary imagery.
Cristo de La Habana
This towering white marble statue of Christ overlooks Havana Bay from across the harbor, offering one of the best panoramic viewpoints of the entire city.
Fortaleza de San Carlos de la Cabaña
This massive 18th-century fortress complex, the largest in the Americas, is famous for its nightly cannon-firing ceremony that draws crowds along its stone ramparts.

dom.op: Ferrocarriles de Cuba — tickets at the Viajero office, no online booking

train.note: Cuba is an island, so there are no international trains. The state railway runs long-distance trains from Havana to Santiago de Cuba, Holguín, Bayamo, Guantánamo and elsewhere, but only roughly every few days and often delayed. There is no online booking for tourists; buy at the Viajero ticket office. Trains currently depart La Coubre station while Havana Central is under renovation.

bus.note: No international buses (island). Viazul is the main long-distance coach line for visitors, linking Havana with Viñales, Varadero, Trinidad, Cienfuegos and Santiago de Cuba, from the Terminal Víazul on Av. 26. Its old viazul.com site is offline; book in person or via the current portal at https://viazul.wetransp.com/.

ferry.note: No scheduled international passenger ferries. Locally, the small Havana harbour launch (lanchita) crosses the bay from the Emboque de Luz terminal to Regla and Casablanca.

half.name: Varadero
half.blurb: Cuba's most famous beach resort, with miles of powdery white sand and turquoise waters.

half.name: Playas del Este
half.blurb: A string of golden beaches just east of the capital, popular with local families.

half.name: Matanzas
half.blurb: A riverside city of bridges, poetry and rumba, dubbed the Athens of Cuba.

half.name: Las Terrazas
half.blurb: An eco-community set in forested hills, with waterfalls, coffee-ruin trails and a serene lake.

half.name: Cojímar
half.blurb: A quaint fishing village that inspired Hemingway's Old Man and the Sea.

full.name: Viñales Valley
full.blurb: A lush UNESCO valley of tobacco farms, dramatic limestone mogotes and traditional cigar-rolling culture.
